## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Describe** the unsupervised clustering problem -- group points by similarity with no
  labels -- and recognize that a clustering is a partition whose labels are arbitrary
  integers, compared with the **adjusted Rand index**. *(Understand)*
- **Explain** K-Means as Lloyd's iteration -- assign each point to its nearest centroid,
  recenter each centroid on its points' mean -- and why it converges, but only to a **local**
  optimum that k-means++ and several runs (`n_init`) guard against. *(Understand)*
- **Apply** K-Means with scikit-learn -- `fit_predict`, `cluster_centers_`, `transform`,
  `predict` -- and read its assignments, distances and Voronoi cells. *(Apply -- in the lab)*
- **Choose** the number of clusters with the elbow and the **silhouette score**, **read a
  silhouette plot**, and explain why inertia cannot choose -- and why the silhouette shares
  K-Means' taste for round clusters. *(Analyze)*
- **Diagnose** K-Means' failure modes -- unscaled features, a bad start, crescents, stretched
  or unequally spread groups -- and **choose a distance metric** that fits the data.
  *(Analyze)*
- **Apply** clustering to real data: compress an image's colors, and pick which examples to
  label for a classifier (semi-supervised learning). *(Apply -- in the lab)*

## Why This Matters

Every algorithm so far -- regression, logistic regression, trees, neural networks -- needed an
answer key: a labeled `y` to learn from. But most data in the world arrives **unlabeled**.
Customers with no segment, photos with no caption, sensor logs with no fault tag. **Unsupervised
learning** asks the question that does not need a teacher: *given only `X`, what structure is
already in the data?*

The first and most common answer is **clustering** -- put similar things together -- and the
whole game turns on one word: **similar**. K-Means gives the simplest possible meaning to it
("close to the same center") and rides that single idea to a fast, scalable algorithm. We build
it, run its loop by hand, learn to choose how many clusters to ask for, find exactly where its
simplicity gives out, and then put it to work: shrinking a photo to 16 colors, and deciding
which 50 of 1347 handwritten digits are worth a human's time to label.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
Imagine dropping 1500 pins on a map and being told to mark four "neighborhoods," with no
addresses or names to go on. You would plant four flags, assign each pin to its nearest flag,
then move each flag to the middle of the pins that chose it -- and repeat until the flags settle.
That is K-Means exactly. "Similar" means "nearest flag"; a neighborhood is just whoever is
closest to the same center.
:::

## From Labels to Structure

Supervised learning fit a map from `X` to a known `y`. Unsupervised learning is handed only
`X` and must find structure on its own. **Clustering** is the canonical task: partition the
points into groups so that members of a group are more similar to each other than to members of
other groups. There is no single right answer and no accuracy to report -- different notions of
"similar" yield different, equally valid clusterings.

Clustering shows up everywhere: **customer segmentation** (group buyers by behavior),
**anomaly detection** (a point far from every cluster is suspicious), **image compression**
(replace each pixel with its cluster's mean color), and **semi-supervised learning** (cluster,
then label a few examples per group). The lab builds the last two. All of them rest on the same
primitive: a way to measure similarity.

## Similarity Is Distance

For K-Means, "similar" means one specific thing: **small Euclidean distance**. The distance
between points $x$ and $x'$ in feature space is

$$
d(x, x') = \lVert x - x' \rVert = \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_j (x_j - x'_j)^2},
$$

and a point belongs to whichever **centroid** -- cluster center -- it is closest to. In the lab,
`transform` reports each point's distance to every centroid, and we turn distance into an
**affinity** with $1/(1+d)$: 1 when you sit on the centroid, fading to 0 as you move away.

Euclidean distance is a choice, not a law. The right notion of "close" depends on what the
features *are*:

| Metric | Distance between $x$ and $x'$ | Data it suits | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Euclidean (L2) | ${\sqrt{\sum_j (x_j-x'_j)^2}}$ | continuous, scaled | straight-line closeness; compact round groups |
| Manhattan (L1) | ${\sum_j \lvert x_j-x'_j \rvert}$ | continuous, grid-like | one big difference should not dominate; many features |
| Chebyshev (L-infinity) | ${\max_j \lvert x_j-x'_j \rvert}$ | continuous | the worst single feature decides (tolerances) |
| Cosine | ${1-x \cdot x' / (\lVert x \rVert \lVert x' \rVert)}$ | text counts, embeddings | direction matters, size does not (long vs short documents) |
| Correlation | ${1-r(x,x')}$ | profiles over time or genes | the *shape* of a profile matters, not its level |
| Jaccard | ${1-\lvert A \cap B \rvert / \lvert A \cup B \rvert}$ | sets, yes/no features | shopping baskets, tags, species present at a site |
| Hamming | share of positions that differ | categorical codes, strings | equal-length codes, DNA sequences, binary flags |
| Mahalanobis | ${\sqrt{(x-x')^{\top} S^{-1}(x-x')}}$ | correlated continuous features | features are correlated or stretched ($S$ = covariance) |

Two practical facts go with the table. First, **scikit-learn's `KMeans` is Euclidean only**:
its update step moves a centroid to the **mean** of its points, and the mean is the point that
minimizes the sum of *squared Euclidean* distances -- for most other metrics (Manhattan, cosine,
Jaccard, ...) the mean is no longer the best center. For cosine, a close stand-in is to scale every row to length 1 first, since
for unit vectors $\lVert x-x' \rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos(x,x')$. For the other metrics you change the
algorithm: the clustering methods of L24 accept a `metric=` argument. Second, almost **every** metric
on raw continuous features (Mahalanobis is the exception) is hijacked by the feature with the largest range, so scale first (more
below). Mahalanobis builds that correction in -- it measures distance in units of the data's own
spread, an idea L25's Gaussian mixtures develop.

## K-Means: The Lloyd Iteration

Given a chosen number of clusters `k`, K-Means runs a beautifully simple loop:

1. **Initialize** `k` centroids (k-means++ picks spread-out starting points -- see below).
2. **Assign** each point to its nearest centroid (the Euclidean similarity rule).
3. **Update** each centroid to the **mean** of the points now assigned to it.
4. Repeat steps 2-3 until the centroids stop moving.

This is **Lloyd's algorithm**. It minimizes the **inertia** -- the within-cluster sum of squared
distances:

$$
\text{inertia} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \; \sum_{x \in C_i} \lVert x - c_i \rVert^2
\qquad (C_i = \text{cluster } i,\; c_i = \text{its centroid})
$$

![Lloyd's algorithm from a deliberately poor start: four centroids (white squares) in a row below the data. Each panel colors the points by their nearest centroid, tints that centroid's cell, and draws an arrow to where the centroid moves when it is recentered on its points' mean (black X). Inertia falls 47,829, 4,734, 1,569, ... and stops at 1,352.2 in iteration 7.](../assets/l23_lloyd_steps.png){#fig-lloyd width="100%" fig-alt="Four scatter plots of the same 1500 points in four blobs. Iteration 1: four white squares sit in a row at x2 = -1 below the data; the plane is split into four vertical strips, the points colored by strip, and long arrows carry each square up to a black X, the mean of its strip, inertia 47,829. Iteration 2: the cells are now slanted regions, arrows are shorter, inertia 4,734. Iteration 3: each centroid sits near a blob center, arrows are tiny, inertia 1,569. Converged at iteration 7: one centroid in the middle of each blob, each blob in its own cell, inertia 1,352.2."}

Each step can only lower the inertia or leave it unchanged: **assign** moves each point to its
nearest centroid, which cannot increase its squared distance, and **update** moves each centroid
to its points' mean, the one spot that minimizes their total squared distance. And there are only
finitely many ways to split `n` points into `k` groups, so the loop cannot keep improving forever
-- it must stop. In the lab, the loop written by hand in NumPy falls from 47,829 to 1,352.2 in
seven passes, exactly the inertia scikit-learn reports (@fig-lloyd).

## Local Optima and the Starting Point

**Convergence is not optimality.** Lloyd only ever goes downhill, so it stops at the bottom of
whatever valley it started in -- a **local optimum**. A bad start can leave two centroids
splitting one true blob while two other blobs share a single centroid; from there no small move
helps, and the loop stays stuck. In the lab, a random start (`init="random"`, one run) on the
four blobs got stuck **12 times in 50** seeds, at inertia about 2,720 against the best 1,352.2.

Two guards, best used together:

- **k-means++** initialization picks the first centroid at random and each next one far from
  those already chosen (with probability proportional to squared distance). It is scikit-learn's
  default, and it cut the stuck runs to **2 in 50**.
- **`n_init`** runs the whole algorithm several times from different starts and keeps the run with
  the lowest inertia. With `n_init=10`, even from random starts, no seed got stuck
  (**0 in 50**). Watch the default:
  since scikit-learn 1.4 it is `n_init="auto"`, which means **one run** when the start is
  k-means++ (and 10 when it is random). Set `n_init=10` yourself when the result matters.

## How Many Clusters?

K-Means cannot tell you `k`; you must supply it. The tempting idea -- pick the `k` with the
smallest inertia -- **fails**, because the best possible inertia *only ever decreases* as `k` grows
(one more centroid can always sit closer to some points; at `k = n` the inertia is zero). A
single Lloyd run can land in a local optimum and break that pattern, but it does not make
inertia a selector. Two honest tools instead:

- **The elbow method.** Plot inertia against `k` and look for the bend where the steep drop
  flattens out. In the lab, inertia plunges from 14,371 to 1,352 by `k=4`, then crawls -- the
  elbow sits at **k=4**, the true number of blobs. It is read by eye: a guide, not a verdict.
- **The silhouette score.** For each point, let $a$ be its mean distance to the other points of
  its own cluster and $b$ its mean distance to the points of the nearest *other* cluster; its
  **silhouette coefficient** is $(b - a)/\max(a, b)$, between $-1$ and $+1$. The **silhouette
  score** is the mean over all points, and you choose the `k` that **maximizes** it. In the lab it
  peaks at **k=4 (0.627)**.

$$
s(x) = \frac{b - a}{\max(a, b)} \qquad
\begin{cases} \;\to +1 & \text{deep inside its cluster} \\ \;\to 0 & \text{on a boundary} \\ \;\to -1 & \text{closer to another cluster} \end{cases}
$$

The silhouette costs more than inertia -- every point is compared with every other point, so the
work grows like $n^2$ -- but it does not simply reward more clusters, so it can actually choose.

One average hides a lot, so look at the **silhouette plot**: every point's coefficient, sorted
within its cluster into a horizontal band (@fig-silhouette).

![Two overlapping blobs clustered with k=2. Left: the points by cluster, with the 5 points whose coefficient is below 0 circled in red -- all on the loose cluster's edge facing the tight one. Right: the silhouette plot; each band is one cluster's coefficients, sorted, one bar per point, so a band's height is the cluster's size (166 and 134 points). The tight cluster's band reaches 0.7 (mean 0.561); the loose cluster's band stops near 0.6 (mean 0.395) and its tail crosses 0. The dashed line is the silhouette score, 0.487.](../assets/l23_silhouette.png){#fig-silhouette width="100%" fig-alt="Left: a scatter of 300 points, an orange tight cluster on the left and a blue loose cluster on the right; five blue points near the border are circled in red, legend s below 0, 5 points. Right: horizontal bar chart of silhouette coefficients from -0.45 to 1. The top orange band, cluster 1 mean 0.561, runs from about 0 to 0.7. The bottom blue band, cluster 0 mean 0.395, runs from about 0.6 down to a short tail below 0. A dashed vertical line marks the silhouette score 0.487."}

The plot has two axes to read. A band's **height** is how many points the cluster has (one thin
bar per point), so bands of very different heights mean clusters of very different sizes. How far
**right** a band reaches is how well its points are placed: a band that stays far to the right is
a cluster whose points sit deep inside it, and a band that slopes toward 0, or whose tail
**crosses 0**, is a cluster with many points near (or past) its border. The single score 0.487
says "decent"; the plot says *which* points are well placed.

::: {.callout-warning title="The silhouette shares K-Means' taste for round clusters"}
The silhouette rewards "close to my cluster, far from the others" -- the same compact, round idea
of a cluster that K-Means uses. On two interleaved crescents (next section) K-Means' **wrong**
split scores **0.489**, while the **true** crescents score only **0.334**: the tips of each
crescent curl closer to the other crescent than to their own far end. So the silhouette is a
fine guide for choosing `k` among compact clusters, but it cannot tell you that K-Means is the
wrong tool for the shape.
:::

## Comparing Clusterings: the Adjusted Rand Index

Cluster numbers are arbitrary, so you cannot score a clustering by checking `labels == y`:
rerun K-Means with another seed and the same blob may be called `2` instead of `0`. The
**adjusted Rand index** (ARI) compares two *groupings* instead. It looks at every pair of points
and asks whether the two groupings agree on "same group" or "different groups", then adjusts for
the agreement chance alone would give. ARI is **1** for identical groupings (whatever the labels'
names), **about 0** for chance-level agreement, and can be slightly negative. In practice you
rarely have true labels -- the lab keeps them aside on synthetic data precisely so it can use ARI
to *measure* what K-Means gets right and wrong. Two runs with different seeds in the lab number
the blobs differently but agree at ARI 0.99 or more.

## When K-Means Breaks

K-Means' single tool -- distance to a center -- carries a hidden assumption: clusters are
**round, compact blobs of similar spread**. Every border between two cells is a straight line,
the set of points equally far from two centroids. When the assumption holds, K-Means is fast
and excellent (ARI **0.962** against the true blobs). When it does not, the failures are
predictable (@fig-cells):

![Voronoi cells. Left: the four blobs, one tinted cell per centroid, with straight borders running between the blobs. Right: the two moons; K-Means' two centroids put one straight border through the middle, so each color takes the end of one crescent and the tip of the other.](../assets/l23_cells_cut.png){#fig-cells width="100%" fig-alt="Two panels. Left: 1500 points in four colored blobs with a black X at each centroid; the plane is tinted in four regions separated by straight lines that pass between the blobs. Right: two interleaved crescents; the plane is split by one slanted straight line into an orange half and a blue half; the orange half holds most of the upper crescent plus the inner tip of the lower one, the blue half holds most of the lower crescent plus the right end of the upper one."}

- **Unscaled features.** Distance is dominated by whatever feature has the largest numeric range.
  If one feature runs 0-1000 and another 0-1, K-Means effectively ignores the small one. In the
  lab, the same data clusters at ARI 0.334 raw versus **1.0 after `StandardScaler`** -- always
  scale first (the standardization of L08/L10).
- **Non-convex shapes.** Two interleaved crescents have clear structure, but one straight border
  cuts across **both**: ARI drops from 0.962 on blobs to **0.239** on the moons. That is not a
  random result -- about **three points in four** (0.745) still land with their own crescent --
  but a structural one: a large piece of each crescent goes to the wrong group, every time.
- **Stretched or unequally spread groups.** Long, slanted groups are cut across by cells built
  around centers (ARI **0.599** on scikit-learn's stretched blobs), and a wide group's outer points
  spill into the cells of tight neighbors, because the border sits halfway between centroids
  regardless of spread (ARI **0.826**). Different *sizes* alone are not the problem when the
  groups are well apart; it is closeness combined with shape or spread.
- **A bad start.** A local optimum (previous section) -- fixed by k-means++ and `n_init`, unlike
  the shape failures, which no number of restarts or extra clusters can fix.

![Which clustering when. Start from the shape of the groups (after scaling the features). Round, compact groups of similar spread, with a guess for k: K-Means. Curved or irregular shapes, unknown k, or outliers to flag: density-based clustering (DBSCAN, L24); if you need the nesting of groups, hierarchical clustering (L24). Stretched groups, or memberships as probabilities: Gaussian mixtures (L25).](../assets/l23_which_clustering.svg){#fig-which width="80%" fig-alt="A decision diagram. The top box asks: what do the groups look like? (scale the features first). An arrow labelled round blobs leads to a blue box, K-Means (this lesson): round, compact groups of similar spread; you can guess k; large data. An arrow labelled curved or irregular leads to a green box, density-based (DBSCAN, L24): any shape; k unknown; outliers flagged as noise. Below it, an arrow labelled need the nesting leads to another green box, hierarchical (L24): nested groups; a whole merge tree to cut at any k. Below K-Means, an arrow labelled stretched, or want probabilities leads to a purple box, Gaussian mixture (L25): elliptical groups; soft, probabilistic memberships."}

The crescents are the cliffhanger into **L24**, where DBSCAN clusters by connected density and
hierarchical clustering merges by linkage, both following the shapes K-Means cuts in two.

## Clustering at Work

**Color quantization.** A color photo is a cloud of points in 3-D color space (red, green, blue).
Cluster the pixels with `k` centroids, repaint each pixel with its centroid's color, and the image
uses only `k` colors (@fig-quantization). Here `k` is not a "true number of groups" -- there is
none -- but a **budget**: the error falls as `k` grows, exactly like inertia, and you stop when the
picture is good enough.

![Color quantization of scikit-learn's sample photo with K-Means: the original (96,615 distinct colors), 4 colors and 16 colors. Each centroid is a mean color; every pixel is repainted with its nearest centroid. Photo: danielbuechele on Flickr, CC BY 2.0, as bundled with scikit-learn.](../assets/l23_quantization.jpg){#fig-quantization width="100%" fig-alt="Three versions of a photo of a Chinese temple among trees under a pale sky. Left: the original. Middle: with 4 colors, the temple is dark brown, the trees dark, the sky pale gray-blue, with flat bands of color. Right: with 16 colors, it is close to the original, with some banding in the sky."}

**Choosing what to label.** Labels cost human time. Clustering can say *which* examples are worth
labeling: cluster the unlabeled data with many clusters, and label only the example nearest each
centroid -- the most typical member of each group. In the lab, with a budget of 50 labels for
1347 handwritten digits, a classifier trained on the **50 representatives** reaches **0.900**
test accuracy, against **0.831** on average for 50 random images (0.736-0.887 over 20 draws) and
0.962 with all 1347 labels. The representatives cover every digit and its common writing styles;
a random draw over-samples some and misses others. This is **semi-supervised learning**: a few
labels, many unlabeled examples, and clustering to connect them. A natural next step,
**label propagation** (copy each representative's label to its whole cluster), is the lab's
Exercise 2 -- and an honest one: on these digits it adds nothing (0.891), as the 7% wrong copied
labels cost about as much as the extra data helps, while in a separate run on 10,000 MNIST digits
(not part of this lab) it lifted accuracy from 0.809 to 0.837.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Reading meaning into cluster numbers.** The labels `0,1,2,3` are arbitrary tags; cluster `0`
  in one run may be cluster `2` in the next. Compare clusterings with the ARI, not their integers.
- **Picking `k` by minimizing inertia.** Inertia falls as clusters are added and bottoms out at
  `k = n`. Use the elbow, the silhouette, and what you know about the problem.
- **Trusting the silhouette as a truth meter.** It shares K-Means' preference for compact, round
  clusters; on curved groups it can prefer the wrong answer.
- **Forgetting to scale.** K-Means is a distance algorithm; an unscaled large-range feature
  hijacks every assignment. Standardize first.
- **Assuming several restarts happen by default.** Since scikit-learn 1.4, `n_init="auto"` runs
  K-Means **once** from a k-means++ start. Pass `n_init=10` when a bad local optimum would hurt.
- **Plugging in another metric.** `KMeans` has no `metric=` argument: its mean-update only fits
  Euclidean distance. Normalize rows for a cosine-like result, or use an algorithm that accepts
  the metric you need.
- **Forcing K-Means on the wrong shape.** If the groups are curved, stretched, nested, or wildly
  different in spread, no amount of tuning fixes the round-blob assumption -- change the
  algorithm.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: why the mean, and why inertia only falls with k (Optional)" collapse="true"}

**Why the mean.** For a set of points $C$, the total squared distance to a center $c$ is
$f(c) = \sum_{x \in C} \lVert x - c \rVert^2$. Setting its gradient to zero,
$\nabla f(c) = -2 \sum_{x \in C} (x - c) = 0$, gives $c = \frac{1}{\lvert C \rvert}\sum_{x \in C} x$:
the mean. So the update step is the exact minimizer of the cluster's inertia -- for **squared
Euclidean** distance only. With Manhattan distance the minimizer is the coordinate-wise
**median**, and for most other metrics there is no simple formula, which is why `KMeans` stays
Euclidean.

**Why the best inertia falls with k.** Take the best clustering with `k` centroids, and add one
more centroid placed exactly on any data point. That point's squared distance drops to 0 and no
other point's distance grows, so the best clustering with `k+1` centroids has inertia at most
that of `k` -- and usually strictly less. That argument is about the *best possible* clustering;
an actual Lloyd run may stop at a local optimum, which is one more reason inertia cannot choose
`k`.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"How do I choose `k` in practice?"** -- Combine signals: the silhouette score across a range of
`k`, a sanity check with the elbow and the silhouette plot, and domain knowledge (you often *know*
you want "3 customer tiers", or have a palette budget). Clustering is exploratory -- there is
rarely one correct `k`.

**"K-Means or something fancier?"** -- K-Means first: it is fast, scalable, and excellent when
clusters are roughly round and you can guess `k`. Reach for DBSCAN (L24) when shapes are
arbitrary or you need outliers flagged, hierarchical clustering when you want a full merge tree,
and Gaussian mixtures (L25) when you want soft, probabilistic memberships (@fig-which).

**"Is clustering the same as classification?"** -- No. Classification learns a labeled `y` and
predicts it; clustering invents groups from `X` alone with no ground truth. You can *use* clusters
afterwards -- as features, as a palette, or to choose what to label -- but the clustering step
itself is unsupervised.

**"Which distance should I use for text?"** -- Usually cosine: two documents about the same topic
point in the same direction in word-count space even if one is ten times longer. Normalize the
rows to length 1 and Euclidean K-Means behaves like a cosine clustering.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Unsupervised learning | find structure in `X` with no labels `y` |
| Clustering | partition points into similar groups; labels are arbitrary integers |
| Similarity (K-Means) | Euclidean **distance to a centroid**; affinity = 1/(1+d) |
| Distance metrics | Euclidean, Manhattan, Chebyshev, cosine, correlation, Jaccard, Hamming, Mahalanobis -- pick by data type |
| Lloyd iteration | assign to nearest centroid, recenter on the mean, repeat until nothing moves |
| Voronoi cells | each centroid's region of the plane; borders are straight lines |
| Inertia | within-cluster sum of squared distances; K-Means minimizes it; falls with `k` |
| Local optimum | where a bad start leaves Lloyd; guards: k-means++ and `n_init` (default: **1** run) |
| Choosing `k` | the **elbow** and the **silhouette score** (maximize it); read the silhouette plot |
| ARI | agreement of two groupings, label names ignored; 1 = same, ~0 = chance |
| Scaling | mandatory -- the largest-range feature hijacks distance otherwise |
| Failure modes | crescents, stretched or unequally spread groups (to L24/L25) |
| At work | color quantization (`k` = palette); label the examples nearest each centroid |
